body_html:
Product listing ads are the image-led product ads that show a photo, price and store name right in Google results. Google now calls them Shopping ads. They run from your product feed in Google Merchant Center, not from keywords, so the quality of your feed largely decides where and how often they appear.

What are product listing ads?

"Product listing ads" (PLAs) is the original name for what Google Ads now labels Shopping ads. Many marketers still use the old term, and it still describes the format well: each ad is a listing for one product, built from data you send to Google.

Instead of writing headlines and choosing keywords, you give Google a structured product feed. Google reads your titles, descriptions, prices, images and identifiers, then decides which searches each product is relevant for. That makes product listing ads closer to a catalog than a classic text ad. Better catalog data means better matching.

Your products can also appear for free. Google Merchant Center lets eligible products show in free listings across Google surfaces such as Search, the Shopping tab, Images and Lens. Paid Shopping ads sit on top of that, giving you more placements and more control.

How do product listing ads work in Google Ads today?

There are two moving parts: Merchant Center, which holds your product data, and Google Ads, which holds your budget and bidding. You link the two accounts, then choose a campaign type.

  • Standard Shopping campaigns run your products only in Shopping placements. You control product groups, bids and campaign priority, which makes them easier to read and adjust.
  • Performance Max campaigns use the same product data but can serve across more of Google's inventory, including Search, YouTube and Discover. Google's own help page notes that any campaign you create inside Merchant Center is a Performance Max campaign.

Neither is right for every store. Standard Shopping gives you clearer reporting and tighter control. Performance Max hands more decisions to Google's automation and can reach more placements. Many stores test both, and it helps to start with the one that matches how much control you want.

How to set up product listing ads, step by step

The setup is not complicated, but the order matters. Skipping the feed work and rushing to launch is the most common reason campaigns stall in their first month.

  1. Create and verify Merchant Center. Add your business details, verify and claim your website, and set up shipping and return policies. Google uses these to judge whether your store is trustworthy.
  2. Add your products. You can connect a platform such as Shopify or WooCommerce, upload a spreadsheet, or use a scheduled feed file. A platform connection keeps prices and stock levels in sync automatically, which prevents many disapprovals.
  3. Fix diagnostics before launch. Merchant Center flags missing attributes, price mismatches and policy problems. Clear the errors first, then work through the warnings.
  4. Link Google Ads. Connect your Google Ads account from Merchant Center. Someone with admin access must approve the link, and Google Ads needs a payment method.
  5. Create the campaign. Google's Shopping campaign setup guide walks through choosing the Merchant Center account, budget, bidding, priority and product groups. Note that you can't change the linked Merchant Center account after the campaign is created.
  6. Set up conversion tracking. Track purchases with revenue values in Google Ads, and check them against GA4. Automated bidding is only as good as the conversion data you give it.

What does a product feed need?

Google's product data specification lists every attribute. The essentials every product needs are:

  • id: a unique identifier for each product, up to 50 characters.
  • title: up to 150 characters.
  • description: up to 5,000 characters.
  • link: the product's landing page URL.
  • image_link: the main product image.
  • availability and price, matching what the landing page shows.

Depending on what you sell, you also need identifiers. Brand is required for most new products. GTIN (the barcode number, such as a UPC) is strongly recommended when your product has one, and Google notes that incorrect or missing GTINs can lead to disapprovals. If a product has no manufacturer GTIN, you supply an MPN instead. Condition is required for used or refurbished items.

Optional attributes like product type, Google product category and custom labels don't get you approved, but they make the campaign far easier to organize later.

How to optimize product listing ads

Once products are live, most gains come from the feed, the structure and the landing pages, roughly in that order.

Write titles for shoppers, not for your warehouse

Your title does the work keywords do in a text ad. Lead with the words people actually search: brand, product type, and the details that matter for that category, such as size, color, material or model number. "Women's Merino Wool Crew Sweater, Navy, Medium" will match more useful searches than an internal SKU name. Check the search terms report regularly and fold the language people use back into titles.

Use images that sell

The image is the first thing a shopper sees. Use a clean, well-lit main image of the product itself. Merchant Center has image rules (no promotional overlays or watermarks on the main image, for example), so follow them, and add extra images with the additional image attribute.

Keep prices and stock accurate

If your feed says one price and your page says another, Google can disapprove the product. Automatic syncing from your store platform, or more frequent feed updates, keeps data current. This matters most during sales.

Structure campaigns around margin and performance

In Standard Shopping, product groups let you split products by brand, category, product type or custom label, then bid differently for each. Custom labels are useful for grouping by margin, season or best sellers. In Performance Max, the equivalent is splitting products across asset groups or campaigns so your best and worst performers don't share one budget.

Add negative keywords where you can

Because Shopping ads match from your feed, they can show for loosely related searches. Review search terms and add negatives in Standard Shopping to stop paying for clicks that will never convert.

Send clicks to a page that closes

The ad gets the click; the product page gets the sale. Make sure the page loads quickly, shows the same price and stock status as the ad, and makes adding to cart obvious on a phone. Measure on profit, not just clicks

Return on ad spend (ROAS) is a useful headline, but compare it with your margins. A high ROAS on low-margin products can still lose money. Reviewing performance by product group every month helps you shift budget toward what actually earns. Clear PPC reporting makes this much faster than digging through the platform.

Are product listing ads right for your business?

They usually fit if you sell physical products online, have a reasonable number of them, and can keep product data accurate. They are a weaker fit if you sell services, custom quotes, or products Google restricts in Shopping. Check Google's Shopping ads policies before you invest time in a feed.

Is "product listing ads" the same as Google Shopping ads?

Yes. Product listing ads is the older name for the format, and Google Ads now calls them Shopping ads. The mechanics are the same: you send product data through Merchant Center, Google matches products to searches, and the ad shows an image, title, price and store name. You'll still see "PLA" used in agency reports and job descriptions, so it's worth knowing both terms refer to the same thing.

Do I need a website to run Shopping ads?

For standard Shopping ads, yes. Each product needs a landing page where a shopper can see the product and buy it, and Google checks that the price and availability on that page match your feed. You also verify and claim your website in Merchant Center. If you don't have an online store yet, building one with clear product pages is the first step.

Should I use Standard Shopping or Performance Max?

It depends on how much control you want. Standard Shopping keeps ads in Shopping placements and lets you manage product groups, bids, priority and negative keywords directly. Performance Max uses the same feed but serves across more of Google and relies more on automation. Many stores start with one, give it enough conversion data to learn, then test the other against it rather than switching back and forth.

Why are my products disapproved in Merchant Center?

The most common reasons are a price or availability mismatch between your feed and landing page, missing or incorrect identifiers such as GTIN or brand, image problems, and policy issues. Merchant Center's diagnostics show the reason for each product. Fix errors at the source, usually your store platform, so the problem doesn't come back with the next feed update, then request a review if needed.
